title: Phase equilibria in MnSb2Te4-GeSb2Te4 system and magnetic properties of Mn1-xGexSb2Te4 solid solutions
authors: Fuad Safarov, Dunya Babanly, Jerome Robert, Elnur Orujlu, Elvin Ahmadov, Martin Bowen, Bohdan Kundys
abstract: As a sister compound of the antiferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4, MnSb2Te4 is also a candidate for exotic magnetic topological phases. On the other hand, the structurally analogous but nonmagnetic phase-change material GeSb2Te4 is also known to exhibit nontrivial band topology. Motivated by their shared crystal structure, the similar ionic radii of Mn2+ and Ge2+, and the opportunity to explore the interplay between magnetism and topology, here we investigate the effects of Ge substitution at Mn sites in MnSb2Te4. The Mn1-xGexSb2Te4 solid solutions were synthesized via high-temperature solid-state reaction and characterized for composition, structure, phase behavior, and magnetism using SEM-EDS, PXRD, DTA, and SQUID. Ge substitution was successful across the full composition range, producing homogeneous, single-phase samples that melt via peritectic reactions, as confirmed by the MnSb2Te4GeS-b2Te4 phase diagram. Ge substitution strengthens the sample's paramagnetism, but with ferrimagnetic ordering up to x = 0.75, with both effective moment and saturation magnetization decreasing with increasing Ge content. Two distinct magnetic transitions - high-temperature paramagnetic to ferrimagnetic and low-temperature ferrimagnetic to ferromagnetic - were identified, with a dome-like shape dependence of the low-temperature magnetic transition on Ge substitution. A negative magnetization was observed in the pristine MnSb2Te4 and x = 0.12 substituted samples, while two distinct spin-flop transitions appeared in the samples with x = 0.32 and x = 0.55 Ge substitutions as a result of competing magnetic orderings. These findings facilitate future selective single-crystal growth of homogeneous, magnetic phases, paving the way for magneto-transport and topological surface states investigations.
summary: This experimental work synthesizes and characterizes $	ext{Mn}_{1-x}	ext{Ge}_x	ext{Sb}_2	ext{Te}_4$ solid solutions to study the interplay between magnetism and topology. By systematically varying Ge content, the researchers mapped out phase equilibria and observed complex magnetic transitions, including spin-flop behavior. These findings are crucial for engineering novel magnetic topological materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the interplay between magnetism and electronic topology by examining how substituting Germanium (Ge) into the $	ext{MnSb}_2	ext{Te}_4$ lattice affects its magnetic and structural properties.
main_result: Ge substitution successfully creates single-phase solid solutions, leading to complex magnetic behavior characterized by multiple transitions, including spin-flop transitions, whose dependence on Ge concentration is systematically mapped out.
method: The research employed a combination of high-temperature solid-state synthesis followed by comprehensive characterization using SQUID magnetometry, PXRD, and DTA.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{MnSb}_2	ext{Te}_4-	ext{GeSb}_2	ext{Te}_4$ solid solution series. The structure is layered (rhombohedral), and the study focuses on how substituting $	ext{Mn}^{2+}$ with $	ext{Ge}^{2+}$ modifies magnetic coupling within this lattice.
key_observables: Saturation magnetization, effective magnetic moment, temperature-dependent magnetic transitions ($	ext{PM} 	o 	ext{FIM} 	o 	ext{FM}$), and the presence of spin-flop transitions.
important_parameters: Ge substitution concentration ($x$), Temperature (2 K to 300 K), Applied Magnetic Field (up to $\pm7$ T).
main_assumptions: The structural integrity is maintained across the full composition range, allowing for the study of magnetic dilution effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temperature profiles during synthesis and magnetization curves showing distinct transitions and spin-flop features as a function of Ge content.
paper_structure: The paper follows a logical progression: first establishing phase equilibria via thermal analysis (DTA) and structure confirmation (PXRD); second, characterizing the magnetic response using SQUID magnetometry across varying compositions; finally, interpreting these results to map out the competition between different magnetic ordering types.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter magnetism/materials science, the study of competing magnetic orderings, field-induced transitions (spin-flop), and topological insulators touches upon complex many-body ground states relevant to correlated electron physics.
